stick_linear_algebra_vectors_and_matrice.question: Linear algebra - vectors and matrices, computed and sealed
references: G. Strang, Introduction to Linear Algebra, 5th ed. (2016)
A. Cayley, A memoir on the theory of matrices, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. 148 (1858) 17
J. W. Gibbs & E. B. Wilson, Vector Analysis (1901) - the dot and cross products
stick_linear_algebra_vectors_and_matrice.statement: Every claim about vectors and matrices is decided by the arithmetic of the vector space axioms: products, norms, angles, determinants, eigenvalues, inverses, solutions.

ticks.claim: [the dot product, SEALED] (1,2,3) . (4,5,6) = 4 + 10 + 18 = 32 (sealed through linear_algebra.LIN_VERIFY): the sum of the componentwise products - a number from two vectors, zero when they are perpendicular.
[the cross product, SEALED] i x j = k (sealed through linear_algebra.LIN_VERIFY): the right-hand rule, a vector perpendicular to both.

[it anticommutes, SEALED] j x i = -k (sealed through linear_algebra.LIN_VERIFY). Reverse the order and the sign flips - the cross product is not commutative, and the engine seals both orders rather than assume one.
[3-4-5, SEALED] |(3,4)| = 5 (sealed through linear_algebra.LIN_VERIFY): Pythagoras as a norm.
[2-3-6-7, SEALED] |(2,3,6)| = sqrt(4 + 9 + 36) = 7 (sealed through linear_algebra.LIN_VERIFY): the theorem in three dimensions, an integer again.
[orthogonal, SEALED] The angle between (1,0) and (0,1) is 90 deg (sealed through linear_algebra.LIN_VERIFY): cos theta = a.b / |a||b| = 0.
[45 degrees, SEALED] Between (1,1) and (1,0): cos theta = 1 / sqrt 2, theta = 45 deg (sealed through linear_algebra.LIN_VERIFY).
[a product, SEALED] [[1,2],[3,4]] [[5,6],[7,8]] = [[19,22],[43,50]] (sealed through linear_algebra.LIN_VERIFY): row times column.

[the reverse product, SEALED] [[5,6],[7,8]] [[1,2],[3,4]] = [[23,34],[31,46]] (sealed through linear_algebra.LIN_VERIFY) - a different matrix. AB is not BA: matrix multiplication is not commutative, and composition of transformations does not care which you did first only when they happen to commute.
[a determinant, SEALED] det [[1,2],[3,4]] = 1 x 4 - 2 x 3 = -2 (sealed through linear_algebra.LIN_VERIFY): the signed area the matrix maps the unit square to; negative means it flips orientation.
[determinants multiply, SEALED] det(AB) = det [[19,22],[43,50]] = 950 - 946 = 4 = (-2)(-2) (sealed through linear_algebra.LIN_VERIFY): det(AB) = det A det B, the area scaling composes.
[singular, SEALED] det [[1,2],[2,4]] = 0 (sealed through linear_algebra.LIN_VERIFY): the rows are dependent, the square is flattened to a line, no inverse exists.
[the trace, SEALED] tr [[1,2],[3,4]] = 5 (sealed through linear_algebra.LIN_VERIFY): the diagonal sum, which equals the sum of the eigenvalues.

[a symmetric matrix, SEALED] The eigenvalues of [[2,1],[1,2]] are 1 and 3 (sealed through linear_algebra.LIN_VERIFY), real, as a symmetric matrix's always are - with eigenvectors (1,-1) and (1,1), perpendicular.

[a rotation, SEALED] The eigenvalues of the 90-degree rotation [[0,-1],[1,0]] are +i and -i (sealed through linear_algebra.LIN_VERIFY): no real vector keeps its direction under a quarter turn, so the eigenvalues leave the real line and sit on the unit circle. The characteristic polynomial is lambda^2 + 1.

[an inverse, SEALED] [[1,2],[3,4]]^-1 = [[-2,1],[1.5,-0.5]] (sealed through linear_algebra.LIN_VERIFY: A times the claimed inverse is the identity). The 2x2 formula: swap the diagonal, negate the off-diagonal, divide by the determinant.

[a rotation's inverse is its transpose, SEALED] [[0,-1],[1,0]]^-1 = [[0,1],[-1,0]] (sealed through linear_algebra.LIN_VERIFY): an orthogonal matrix undoes itself by transposition, because rotating back is rotating the other way.
[a solved system, SEALED] [[1,2],[3,4]] x = (5,11) has x = (1,2) (sealed through linear_algebra.LIN_VERIFY: A x reproduces b). Two equations, two unknowns, a nonzero determinant - exactly one answer.

[the axioms, CITED] A vector space is eight axioms over a field (closure, associativity, commutativity of addition, zero, negatives, and the two distributive and two scalar laws); a matrix is a linear map written in a basis (Cayley 1858). Cited, never sealed - every computation above is a theorem of them, decided by arithmetic.
ticks.source: Strang, Introduction to Linear Algebra (2016); Cayley, Phil. Trans. 148 (1858) 17

ticks.claim: [the bound, stated] The verifier rests on numpy, the optional math extra: on a stdlib-only box it returns NOT_APPLICABLE and never a false result, so this stick is minted where numpy lives. Exact comparisons are at 1e-6 relative; a half-degree window on angles.

[on the one map] Linear algebra is the grammar of the change of domain (the change-of-domain stick: an eigenbasis is the axis where a matrix is diagonal), of the SVD (rotation, stretch, rotation), of tensors (the invariants under a change of basis), and of quantum mechanics (card_floor_quantum_mechanics: a Hermitian matrix's real eigenvalues are the observables; a unitary's unit-circle eigenvalues are the phases - the rotation sealed above is the simplest). Where two domains connect, there is a matrix between them.
